l: Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 27
s: Babylon is the land of the king Nebuchadnezzar, to whom the LORD has given the nations. The remaining temple vessels will be carried there and remain until the LORD visits them and brings them back, and Jeremiah says that the vessels taken earlier will not shortly be returned from Babylon as some prophets claim.

l: false prophets (of Judah and the nations), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 27
s: Prophets, diviners, dreamers, soothsayers, and sorcerers are said to tell the nations and Judah not to serve the king of Babylon, which the LORD calls a lie meant to remove them from their land and cause them to perish. The LORD says he has not sent them, that they prophesy falsely in his name, and that some claim the temple vessels will soon return from Babylon. Jeremiah challenges them to intercede so the remaining vessels don't go to Babylon.

l: nations (under Nebuchadnezzar's yoke), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 27
s: The kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon receive the message through their messengers in Jerusalem. All nations are told they will serve Nebuchadnezzar, his son, and his son's son; those who submit will stay in their land and till it, while those who refuse will be punished with sword, famine, and pestilence. Later, many nations and great kings will make Babylon's king their bondservant.

l: bonds and bars (Jeremiah's yoke), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 27
s: The LORD instructs Jeremiah to make bonds and bars and put them on his neck. They serve as the sign accompanying the message sent to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon that they should put their necks under Babylon's yoke.

l: vessels (of the LORD's house), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 27
s: Prophets claim the vessels of the LORD's house will shortly be brought back from Babylon, but the LORD says this is a lie. The pillars, the sea, the bases, and the remaining vessels in the temple, the king's house, and Jerusalem, which Nebuchadnezzar did not take earlier, will be carried to Babylon and stay there until the LORD visits them, then brings them up and restores them to this place.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 28
s: In the fourth year of Zedekiah's reign, the prophet Hananiah the son of Azzur declares in the LORD's house that the LORD has broken the yoke of the king of Babylon and that within two years the temple vessels and Jeconiah with all the captives will return. Jeremiah answers 'Amen' but warns that a prophet of peace is only known as true when his word comes to pass. Hananiah then takes the bar from Jeremiah's neck and breaks it, repeating his two-year promise. The LORD tells Jeremiah that wooden bars have been replaced by iron ones, meaning all the nations will serve Nebuchadnezzar. Jeremiah tells Hananiah the LORD has not sent him and that he will die that year, and Hananiah dies in the seventh month.

l: Hananiah the son of Azzur, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 28
s: Hananiah, a prophet from Gibeon, spoke in the LORD's house before the priests and people, claiming the LORD had broken Babylon's yoke and would return the vessels and captives within two years. He broke the bar from Jeremiah's neck, and was told by Jeremiah that the LORD had not sent him and that he made the people trust a lie. He died that same year in the seventh month.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 28
s: Jeremiah, wearing a neck bar, responded to Hananiah with 'Amen' but cautioned that a prophet of peace is proved only when his word happens. After Hananiah broke the bar, Jeremiah went his way, then received the LORD's word and told Hananiah that iron bars replaced the wooden ones and that he would die that year. His words were fulfilled when Hananiah died in the seventh month.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 28
s: The LORD, according to Hananiah, had broken the yoke of Babylon's king, though the LORD told Jeremiah he had not sent Hananiah. He declared he had put an iron yoke on all these nations to serve Nebuchadnezzar, and he sentenced Hananiah to die within the year for speaking rebellion against him.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 28
s: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is said to have taken the vessels of the LORD's house to Babylon. Hananiah falsely claimed his yoke would be broken in two years, but the LORD said all the nations would serve him, and that he was also given the animals of the field.

l: Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 28
s: Babylon is the place where the temple vessels and the captives of Judah, including Jeconiah, were taken. Hananiah prophesied their return from there, while the LORD declared the nations would serve Babylon's king.

l: the LORD’s house, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 28
s: The LORD's house is the setting where Hananiah and Jeremiah spoke before the priests and all the people. Its vessels had been carried to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, and Hananiah promised their return within two years.

l: yoke of the king of Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 28
s: Hananiah claimed the LORD had broken the yoke of the king of Babylon and would break it from all nations within two years. The LORD countered through Jeremiah that he had put a yoke of iron on all these nations so they would serve Nebuchadnezzar.

l: bar (Jeremiah's neck bar), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 28
s: The bar on Jeremiah's neck was taken off and broken by Hananiah in front of the people as a sign of his prophecy. The LORD said the broken wooden bars were replaced by bars of iron.

l: Hananiah's prophecy of peace, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 28
s: Hananiah's prophecy promised that within two full years the vessels, Jeconiah, and all the captives would return from Babylon. Jeremiah said it would be tested by whether it happened, and the LORD called it a lie and rebellion, with Hananiah dying that same year.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: Jeremiah the prophet sends a letter from Jerusalem, carried by Elasah and Gemariah, to the exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar took to Babylon. In it the LORD tells them to build houses, plant gardens, marry, multiply, and seek the peace of Babylon, warning them not to trust their prophets and diviners, and promising a return after seventy years. The LORD also declares judgment of sword, famine, and pestilence on the king and the people remaining in Jerusalem, who are likened to rotten figs. He announces that Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who prophesy lies, will be delivered to Nebuchadnezzar and killed. Shemaiah the Nehelamite sends letters urging the priests to rebuke Jeremiah, and the LORD pronounces punishment on Shemaiah and his offspring for speaking rebellion.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: Jeremiah the prophet sends a letter from Jerusalem to the exiles in Babylon. Shemaiah's letter attacks him as a self-appointed prophet, and Zephaniah the priest reads that letter in his hearing. The LORD then gives Jeremiah a message of judgment against Shemaiah to send to the captives.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: The LORD instructs the captives to settle in Babylon and seek its peace, and promises to bring them back after seventy years with thoughts of peace and a future. He declares he did not send the false prophets, and pronounces judgment on the king and people remaining in Jerusalem, on Ahab and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, and on Shemaiah. He presents himself as the one who knows and is witness.

l: Jeremiah's letter, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: The letter is carried to Babylon by Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Nebuchadnezzar. It is addressed to the elders, priests, prophets, and all the people taken captive. Its message is to settle, multiply, seek Babylon's peace, and not heed false prophets, with a promise of return. Shemaiah later cites its words, "The captivity is long. Build houses," as grounds for rebuking Jeremiah.

l: deportations of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: The captives, including elders, priests, prophets, and people carried off after Jeconiah and the craftsmen departed, are told to build, plant, marry, multiply, and pray for the city. They are warned not to listen to their prophets, diviners, or dreams. They are promised that the LORD will hear them when they seek him with all their heart and will gather them from all nations.

l: Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: Babylon is the place where the LORD has caused the Judeans to be carried captive. The captives are told to seek its peace and pray for it, since in its peace they will have peace. Its time is limited to seventy years, after which the LORD will visit the exiles.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: Jerusalem is the city from which Jeremiah sends his letter and from which the exiles were taken. The king on David's throne and the people still living there face sword, famine, and pestilence. Shemaiah sends letters to Zephaniah and the priests there, urging them to discipline Jeremiah.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is the one who carried the Judeans away captive. Zedekiah king of Judah sends envoys to him in Babylon. The LORD says he will deliver Ahab and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah into his hand, and that he will kill them before the captives' eyes, roasting them in fire.

l: false prophets and diviners, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: The captives are warned that the prophets and diviners among them prophesy falsely in the LORD's name, though he did not send them. Ahab, Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, and Shemaiah are named as examples. The LORD says earlier prophets he sent were not listened to, and the people's claim that he raised up prophets in Babylon is rebuked.

l: seventy years, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: The LORD states that after seventy years are accomplished for Babylon, he will visit the exiles and perform his good word. This will cause them to return to Jerusalem. The period frames the long stay in Babylon that the letter tells them to settle into.

l: return from captivity, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: The LORD promises to turn again the captivity, gather the exiles from all nations and places where he drove them, and bring them back to the place they were carried from. This follows seventy years and depends on them calling on him and seeking him with all their heart. Shemaiah will not see the good the LORD will do for his people.

l: people remaining in Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: The king on David's throne and the brothers who did not go into captivity are said to face the sword, famine, and pestilence. The LORD will make them like rotten figs that cannot be eaten. He will scatter them among all the kingdoms to be an object of horror, a hissing, and a reproach, because they did not listen to his prophets.

l: Ahab the son of Kolaiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: Ahab son of Kolaiah is named as one who prophesies a lie in the LORD's name. The LORD will deliver him into Nebuchadnezzar's hand to be killed before the captives. His fate, being roasted in the fire by the king of Babylon, will become a curse formula among the exiles. He is also accused of committing adultery with his neighbors' wives.

l: Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: Zedekiah son of Maaseiah is named with Ahab as prophesying a lie in the LORD's name. The LORD will deliver him to Nebuchadnezzar, who will kill him before the captives' eyes, and his fate will be used in a curse. He is accused of foolish acts, adultery with his neighbors' wives, and speaking words the LORD did not command.

l: Shemaiah the Nehelamite, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: Shemaiah sends letters in his own name to Zephaniah the priest and the priests in Jerusalem, urging them to put Jeremiah in the stocks and shackles as a madman posing as a prophet. The LORD declares that Shemaiah prophesied without being sent and led the people to trust a lie. He and his offspring will be punished, none will remain among the people, and he will not see the good the LORD will do.

l: Jeremiah's instructions to settle in Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 29
s: The LORD's instructions tell the exiles to build houses, plant gardens and eat their fruit, take wives, have children, arrange marriages for their sons and daughters, and multiply rather than diminish. They are also to seek the city's peace and pray for it. Shemaiah quotes these instructions in his complaint against Jeremiah.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 30
s: In Jeremiah 30, the LORD tells Jeremiah to write all his words in a book and promises to reverse the captivity of Israel and Judah and return them to the land given to their fathers. He describes a terrifying day, the time of Jacob's trouble, from which Jacob will be saved, when he will break the yoke of foreign rule and raise up David their king. The LORD explains that Israel's wound is incurable and that he inflicted it because of the greatness of their iniquity, with their former lovers forgetting them. He promises nonetheless to devour and plunder those who devoured and plundered Israel, to heal Israel, and to rebuild its city and multiply its people. The chapter closes with the promise that they will be his people, and that his fierce anger will burst on the wicked and not return until he has accomplished his purposes.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 30
s: The LORD commands Jeremiah to write all his words in a book and promises to reverse the captivity of Israel and Judah, break the yoke of their oppressors, and heal Israel's wounds. He says he caused Israel's wound because of their iniquity, will correct them in measure without leaving them unpunished, and will make a full end of the nations where he scattered them but not of Israel. He declares "You shall be my people, and I will be your God," and sends a sweeping storm of wrath on the wicked that will not return until he has performed the intentions of his heart.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 30
s: Israel, together with Judah, is promised a return from captivity to the land given to their fathers, where they will possess it. Its wound is called incurable and is attributed to the greatness of its iniquity, yet it is told not to be dismayed, since the LORD will save, heal, multiply, and glorify it. They will serve the LORD and David their king, and will be his people.

l: Jacob, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 30
s: Jacob is addressed as the LORD's servant and told not to fear, for the LORD will save him from afar along with his offspring. Although he faces a time of trouble, he will be saved out of it, and will return to be quiet and at ease with no one making him afraid. His tents will see the captivity reversed and his dwelling places receive compassion.

l: restoration of Israel (return from exile), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 30
s: The LORD promises to reverse the captivity of his people Israel and Judah and bring them back to the land he gave their fathers. He will save them and their offspring from the land of their captivity, and will reverse the captivity of Jacob's tents. Those who enslave them will themselves go into captivity.

l: restoration (of Israel), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 30
s: The LORD promises restoration: breaking the yoke and bonds so strangers no longer enslave them, restoring health and healing wounds, and building the city on its own hill with the palace in its own place. Thanksgiving and merry voices will come from them, they will be multiplied and glorified, their children will be as before, and their congregation established before the LORD. Their prince and ruler will come from among them and be brought near to the LORD.

l: time of Jacob's trouble, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 30
s: The day is described as great, with none like it, marked by a voice of trembling and fear, and men with hands on their waists like a woman in labor with faces turned pale. It is called the time of Jacob's trouble, but Jacob will be saved out of it. On that day the LORD will break the yoke from the neck and burst the bonds.

l: enemies and oppressors (of Israel), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 30
s: Strangers who have made Israel bondservants will do so no more, as the LORD breaks their yoke. All who devour, plunder, and prey on Israel will be devoured, plundered, and made prey, and all adversaries will go into captivity. The LORD says he will punish all who oppress them and make a full end of the nations where he scattered Israel, and his wrath will burst on the head of the wicked.

l: wound (Israel's incurable wound), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 30
s: The LORD declares Israel's hurt incurable and its wound grievous, with no one to plead its cause and no healing medicines. He says he inflicted it as the wound of an enemy, the chastisement of a cruel one, and Israel's lovers have forgotten it. Yet he promises to restore health and heal the wounds, because others have called Zion an outcast whom no one seeks.

l: iniquity (Israel's sin), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 30
s: The text states twice that the greatness of Israel's iniquity and the increase of its sins is the reason the LORD wounded and chastised it. This is given as the reason Israel's pain is incurable and should not be cried over. The LORD says he will correct Israel in measure and will in no way leave it unpunished.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 31
s: In Jeremiah 31, the LORD promises to be God of all the families of Israel and to rebuild, regather, and ransom Jacob/Israel from the north and the uttermost parts of the earth, turning mourning into joy. Rachel weeps in Ramah for her children, but the LORD tells her to stop weeping because they will return, and he expresses mercy and yearning for repentant Ephraim, his dear son. The LORD announces that he will sow the houses of Israel and Judah, watch over them to build and plant, and end the proverb about sour grapes so that each dies for his own iniquity. He promises a new covenant with Israel and Judah, unlike the one made when he brought their fathers out of Egypt, by writing his law on their hearts and forgiving their iniquity. He guarantees Israel's permanence as long as the sun, moon, stars, and heavens endure, and foretells Jerusalem rebuilt and holy to the LORD, never to be plucked up again.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 31
s: The LORD promises to be God of all the families of Israel, declares his everlasting love, and vows to gather, ransom, lead, and comfort his people as a father and shepherd. He announces a new covenant, pledges to forgive iniquity and remember sin no more, and swears that Israel will not be cast off while the heavens and earth's foundations remain unmeasured. He describes himself as the one who gives the sun, moon, and stars and is called the LORD of Armies.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 31
s: Israel, also called Jacob, Ephraim, and the virgin of Israel, is promised rebuilding, joy, planting of vineyards, and return from the north and distant lands as a great company. Ephraim repents of the reproach of his youth and is called the LORD's firstborn and dear son, and Rachel's weeping for her children is answered with a promise of their return. The LORD says Israel's offspring will not cease being a nation before him as long as the sun, moon, and stars' ordinances continue.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 31
s: Judah and its cities are promised that, when the LORD reverses their captivity, people will bless it as a habitation of righteousness and mountain of holiness. Farmers and shepherds will dwell there together. The LORD will sow the house of Judah along with the house of Israel and make a new covenant with both.

l: new covenant, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 31
s: The LORD declares he will make a new covenant with the houses of Israel and Judah, not like the one made with their fathers when he brought them out of Egypt, which they broke. In it he will put his law in their inward parts and write it on their hearts, they will all know him from least to greatest, and he will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more.

l: restoration of Israel (return from exile), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 31
s: The LORD promises to bring Israel back from the north country and the ends of the earth, including the blind, lame, and women with child, weeping but led by rivers in a straight way. They will sing on Zion, enjoy grain, wine, and oil, and see mourning turned to joy, while the city is rebuilt from the tower of Hananel onward and the whole valley and fields to the Kidron become holy and never again plucked up.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: In the tenth year of Zedekiah, with Babylon's army besieging Jerusalem, Jeremiah is imprisoned in the court of the guard by King Zedekiah for prophesying that the city and the king will fall to Babylon. At the LORD's word, Jeremiah's cousin Hanamel offers him the field at Anathoth, and Jeremiah buys it for seventeen shekels of silver, signs and seals the deed before witnesses, and gives it to Baruch to store in an earthen vessel as a sign that fields will again be bought in the land. Jeremiah then prays, praising the LORD's power and history with Israel and puzzling over the command to buy land when the city is about to fall to the Chaldeans. The LORD answers that nothing is too hard for him, confirms that Jerusalem will be burned because of Judah's and Israel's idolatry and disobedience, and then promises to regather the people, make an everlasting covenant with them, and reverse their captivity so that fields are bought again throughout the land.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: Jeremiah is shut up in the court of the guard by Zedekiah for prophesying Jerusalem's fall. At the LORD's word he buys his cousin Hanamel's field at Anathoth, has the deed witnessed and entrusted to Baruch, and then prays, wondering at the command to buy land while the city is falling. The LORD answers him with judgment on the city and a promise of restoration.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: The LORD tells Jeremiah that Hanamel will come, and commands the deeds to be preserved in an earthen vessel as a sign that land will be bought again. He declares that nothing is too hard for him, that he will give Jerusalem to the Chaldeans because of the people's evil, and that he will afterward regather them, make an everlasting covenant, and reverse their captivity.

l: Zedekiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: Zedekiah, king of Judah, has shut Jeremiah in the court of the guard for prophesying that the city will fall. The prophecy states that he will not escape the Chaldeans but will be delivered to the king of Babylon, speak with him mouth to mouth, and be taken to Babylon until the LORD visits him.

l: Hanamel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: Hanamel, son of Shallum and Jeremiah's uncle's son, comes to Jeremiah in the court of the guard as the LORD had foretold. He asks Jeremiah to buy his field in Anathoth under the right of redemption, and he is present when the deed is delivered to Baruch.

l: Baruch the son of Neriah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: Baruch, son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, receives the sealed and open deeds of purchase from Jeremiah before Hanamel, the witnesses, and the Jews in the court of the guard. He is commanded to put them in an earthen vessel so they will last many days.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: Jerusalem is under siege, with siege ramps built against it, and the LORD says he will give it to the Chaldeans and Nebuchadnezzar, who will set it on fire. Its judgment is tied to its long provocation of the LORD, including incense to Baal and abominations in the house called by his name. The LORD nevertheless promises that people will dwell safely in the land again and buy fields around Jerusalem.

l: Chaldeans, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: The Chaldeans, under Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, are besieging Jerusalem and have built siege ramps against it. The LORD says the city is given into their hand and that they will come, set it on fire, and burn it with the houses where incense was offered to Baal.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: The LORD says the children of Israel, together with Judah, have done only evil from their youth and provoked him with the work of their hands. Jeremiah recalls how the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt with signs and wonders and gave them the land. The LORD promises to gather them from all countries, be their God, give them one heart and one way, and make an everlasting covenant.

l: people of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: The people of Judah, with their kings, princes, priests, and prophets, are charged with turning their backs on the LORD, ignoring his teaching, defiling his house with abominations, and building high places of Baal in the valley of the son of Hinnom to pass their children through fire to Molech. The LORD promises that they will be regathered, given one heart, and planted in the land, and that their captivity will be reversed.

l: field at Anathoth, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: The field at Anathoth, in the land of Benjamin, belongs to Hanamel and is offered to Jeremiah under the right of redemption and inheritance. Jeremiah buys it for seventeen shekels of silver. It serves as a sign that fields will again be bought in the land despite the coming Chaldean conquest.

l: deed of purchase, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: Jeremiah signs and seals the deed, with one sealed copy containing the terms and conditions and one open copy, and has it witnessed. He gives it to Baruch with the instruction to put both deeds in an earthen vessel so they will last many days, as a sign that houses, fields, and vineyards will be bought again.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: The king of Babylon's army is besieging Jerusalem in the tenth year of Zedekiah and the eighteenth of Nebuchadnezzar, with siege ramps built against the city. Jeremiah says it has come about through sword, famine, and pestilence, and the LORD confirms the city will be taken and burned.

l: restoration of the captivity, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 32
s: The LORD promises to gather the people from all countries where he drove them and bring them back to dwell safely. He says he will be their God, give them one heart and one way, make an everlasting covenant, and plant them in the land with his whole heart. Just as he brought the evil, he will bring the promised good, and fields will be bought, deeds signed and sealed, and witnesses called throughout Benjamin, Judah, and the surrounding places as captivity is reversed.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 33
s: The LORD speaks to Jeremiah a second time while he is still locked up in the court of the guard. He promises that Jerusalem and Judah, though now broken down and desolate from the Chaldeans' attack, will receive health, healing, cleansing, and pardon. The LORD says the voices of joy, bridegroom and bride, and thanksgiving will return, flocks will again be counted in the cities, and the captivity will be reversed as at the first. He promises a Branch of righteousness to grow up to David, and that David will never lack a man on the throne nor the Levitical priests a man to offer sacrifices. He ties these promises to his covenant of day and night, saying that only if it could be broken could his covenant with David and the Levites fail, and he rebukes those who say he has cast off the two families.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 33
s: The LORD speaks to Jeremiah, invites people to call on him, and promises health, healing, cleansing, pardon, and reversal of the captivity for Judah and Israel. He pledges to raise up a Branch of righteousness for David, to multiply David's offspring and the Levites, and to keep his covenant as surely as he keeps day and night.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 33
s: Jeremiah is still locked up in the court of the guard when the LORD's word comes to him a second time. He receives three further messages in this chapter, each introduced by the LORD's word coming to him.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 33
s: Jerusalem is described as a desolate place without man or animal, with houses broken down against the Chaldean mounds. The LORD promises it health, healing, peace, and truth, says it will dwell safely, and says it will be called 'The LORD our righteousness' and be a name of joy, praise, and glory before the nations.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 33
s: Judah's cities are called waste, but the LORD promises to restore its fortunes, bring back joy and thanksgiving, and let shepherds and flocks fill its cities again. In the days of the Branch, Judah will be saved.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 33
s: The LORD promises to restore the fortunes of Judah and Israel and build them as at the first, and to perform his good word concerning the house of Israel. Israel is also the throne over which David will never lack a man to sit.

l: David, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 33
s: The LORD promises that a Branch of righteousness will grow up to David and that David will never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel. His offspring will be multiplied like the army of the sky and the sand of the sea, and the LORD calls him 'my servant'.

l: righteous Branch (of David), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 33
s: The LORD says he will cause a Branch of righteousness to grow up to David in those days. The Branch will execute justice and righteousness in the land.

l: Levitical priests, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 33
s: The LORD promises that the Levitical priests will never lack a man before him to offer burnt offerings, burn meal offerings, and do sacrifice continually. He also promises to multiply the Levites who minister to him, and calls them his ministers.

l: covenant of day and night, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 33
s: The LORD points to his covenant of day and night as the guarantee of his covenant with David and the Levitical priests: only if it could be broken could those covenants be broken. He repeats that if it fails, he would cast away the offspring of Jacob and David, but he will instead reverse their captivity and have mercy.

l: restoration of the captivity, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 33
s: The LORD repeatedly promises to reverse the captivity of the land and of Judah and Israel, so that things will be as at the first. It is tied to renewed joy, thanksgiving in the LORD's house, flocks in the cities, and mercy on the offspring of Jacob and David.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: While Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his army fight against Jerusalem and the remaining cities of Judah, the LORD sends Jeremiah to tell King Zedekiah that the city will be burned and that he will be taken to Babylon, though he will die in peace. The chapter then recounts how Zedekiah made a covenant with the people of Jerusalem to free their Hebrew male and female servants, and how the princes and people first obeyed but then took the servants back. The LORD recalls his covenant with their fathers at the exodus from Egypt requiring release of Hebrew servants after seven years, and charges the people with profaning his name by reversing their release. As punishment he proclaims a 'liberty' to the sword, pestilence, and famine, and gives the covenant-breakers, including Zedekiah and his princes, into the hands of their enemies. He declares that the Babylonian army will return to take and burn Jerusalem and make the cities of Judah a desolation.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: The LORD sends Jeremiah to announce to Zedekiah that Jerusalem will be given to the king of Babylon and burned, while promising Zedekiah a peaceful death. He recalls his covenant with the fathers at the exodus requiring release of Hebrew servants after seven years, and accuses the people of profaning his name by taking back their freed servants. He pronounces judgment: a 'liberty' to sword, pestilence, and famine, and a command that the Babylonian army return to take and burn the city and desolate Judah's cities.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: Jeremiah receives the word of the LORD and speaks all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah in Jerusalem while the Babylonian army fights against the city. He then receives further words from the LORD condemning the people for reversing the release of their servants.

l: Zedekiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: Zedekiah is told he will not escape Babylon's hand, will be taken, will see the king of Babylon face to face, and will go to Babylon, yet will die in peace with burnings made for him like his royal predecessors. He had made a covenant with the people of Jerusalem to proclaim liberty to Hebrew servants, and is later named among those to be given into the hands of enemies and the Babylonian army.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, with all his army and the kingdoms and peoples under his dominion, is fighting against Jerusalem and all its cities. The LORD declares he will be given Jerusalem and will burn it with fire, and that he will speak with Zedekiah mouth to mouth.

l: Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: Babylon is the place to which Zedekiah will be taken, and its king is the one into whose hand the LORD will give Jerusalem. Its army is said to have gone away from the city but will be commanded by the LORD to return.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: Jerusalem is under attack by the king of Babylon's army, and the LORD declares it will be given to the king of Babylon and burned with fire. It is where Zedekiah made the covenant of liberty with the people, and the army will return to fight against it, take it, and burn it.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: Judah's cities are under attack, with only Lachish and Azekah remaining as fortified cities. The LORD declares he will make the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant, and its princes and people are condemned for breaking the covenant.

l: Babylon's army, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: The army is fighting against Jerusalem and the remaining cities of Judah, including Lachish and Azekah. It has gone away from the city, but the LORD says he will command it to return, fight against Jerusalem, take it, and burn it with fire.

l: people of Jerusalem and Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: The princes and people entered the covenant and at first obeyed by freeing their Hebrew male and female servants, but afterwards turned and forced them back into servitude. The LORD accuses them of profaning his name and breaking the covenant made by passing between the parts of a cut calf, and declares they will be given to their enemies, with their dead bodies becoming food for birds and animals.

l: servants (Hebrew bondservants), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: The Hebrew male and female servants were released under the covenant so that no one would keep a fellow Jew as a bondservant. After they were let go, their masters caused them to return and brought them back into subjection as servants and handmaids.

l: covenant of liberty for servants, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: Zedekiah made this covenant with all the people in Jerusalem, made before the LORD in the house called by his name, to free every Hebrew male and female servant. It echoes the LORD's earlier covenant at the exodus requiring release after seven years, but the people broke it by retaking their servants, which brings judgment on the covenant-breakers who had passed between the parts of the calf.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 34
s: Nebuchadnezzar's forces are fighting against Jerusalem and the remaining fortified cities of Judah, Lachish and Azekah, as the chapter opens. The LORD declares the city will fall and be burned, and that the army, though it has gone away, will be commanded to return and take it.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 35
s: In the days of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, the LORD tells Jeremiah to bring the Rechabites into the LORD's house and offer them wine. Jeremiah gathers Jaazaniah, his brothers, his sons, and the whole house of the Rechabites into a room and sets bowls and cups of wine before them. They refuse, saying their father Jonadab son of Rechab commanded them never to drink wine, build houses, sow seed, or plant vineyards, but to live in tents, and that they came to Jerusalem only for fear of the Babylonian and Syrian armies. The LORD uses their faithfulness as a contrast, telling Jeremiah to ask the men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem why they do not listen to him, and announces that he will bring on them all the evil he has pronounced. Jeremiah then tells the Rechabites that because they obeyed Jonadab, Jonadab will never lack a man to stand before the LORD.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 35
s: Jeremiah receives the LORD's word in the days of Jehoiakim and brings the Rechabites into the LORD's house, setting wine before them and telling them to drink. He then delivers the LORD's message of judgment to Judah and Jerusalem and announces the LORD's promise to the Rechabites.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 35
s: The LORD commands Jeremiah to test the Rechabites with wine, then uses their obedience to rebuke Judah for ignoring his repeated warnings through the prophets. He pronounces coming evil on Judah and Jerusalem and promises that Jonadab son of Rechab will never lack a man to stand before him.

l: Rechabites, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 35
s: The Rechabites, led by Jaazaniah son of Jeremiah and his brothers and sons, are brought into the LORD's house and refuse the wine offered to them. They explain that they live in tents and keep Jonadab's commands, and that they came to Jerusalem only for fear of the Chaldean and Syrian armies. The LORD promises them, through Jeremiah, a continuing line before him.

l: Jonadab the son of Rechab, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 35
s: Jonadab son of Rechab is the Rechabites' father, who commanded them and their children never to drink wine, build houses, sow seed, or plant vineyards, but to dwell in tents. The LORD promises that he will not lack a man to stand before him forever.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 35
s: Judah is the land of King Jehoiakim, where the Rechabites live as nomads and which Nebuchadnezzar enters. The LORD declares he will bring on Judah and all Jerusalem's inhabitants the evil he has pronounced, because they did not listen or answer.

l: inhabitants of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 35
s: The men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem are accused of refusing instruction and not heeding the LORD, who rose early to speak to them and sent the prophets calling them to turn from evil and from other gods. Unlike the Rechabites, they have not listened, and the LORD announces that he will bring on them all the evil he pronounced.

l: the LORD's house, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 35
s: The LORD's house is where Jeremiah brings the Rechabites, into the room of the sons of Hanan son of Igdaliah, the man of God, beside the princes' room and above the room of Maaseiah son of Shallum, the keeper of the threshold. It is the setting for the wine test.

l: wine, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 35
s: Wine is set before the Rechabites in bowls and cups at the LORD's command as a test, and they refuse it because of Jonadab's prohibition. Their refusal shows faithful obedience in contrast to Judah's disobedience.

l: Rechabite obedience to Jonadab's commands, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 35
s: The Rechabites have kept all of Jonadab's commands: no wine, no houses, no fields, vineyards, or seed, and life in tents, for them, their wives, sons, and daughters. The LORD holds this obedience up against Judah's failure to listen to him and rewards it with a promise that Jonadab will always have a man to stand before him.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 36
s: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the LORD told Jeremiah to write all his words against Israel, Judah, and the nations on a scroll, hoping Judah would repent. Jeremiah dictated it to Baruch the son of Neriah and sent him to read it in the LORD's house on a fast day, since Jeremiah was restricted. After Baruch read it in the fifth year, the princes heard it, feared, told Baruch and Jeremiah to hide, and reported it to the king. Jehoiakim had Jehudi read the scroll, cut it up with a penknife and burned it in the brazier, showing no fear, and ordered the arrest of Baruch and Jeremiah, but the LORD hid them. The LORD then had Jeremiah write a second scroll with Baruch and pronounced judgment on Jehoiakim: no heir on David's throne, and his body cast out to heat and frost.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 36
s: Jeremiah receives the LORD's command to put all his words on a scroll and dictates them to Baruch. Being restricted from the LORD's house, he sends Baruch to read it, and after the king burns the scroll he is sought for arrest but hidden by the LORD. He then dictates a second scroll with many similar words added.

l: Baruch the son of Neriah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 36
s: Baruch writes Jeremiah's dictated words on a scroll and reads it in the LORD's house, and later before the princes, explaining that he wrote with ink from Jeremiah's mouth. He is told to hide, is targeted for arrest by the king, is hidden by the LORD, and writes the second scroll.

l: Jehoiakim, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 36
s: Jehoiakim hears the scroll read, cuts it with a penknife and burns it in the brazier, showing no fear and ignoring the intercession of Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah. He orders Jeremiah and Baruch arrested. The LORD declares he will have no one to sit on David's throne, his body will be cast out to heat and frost, and he, his offspring, and his servants will be punished.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 36
s: The LORD commands Jeremiah to write the scroll in hope that Judah will repent and be forgiven. He hides Baruch and Jeremiah from the king, commands a replacement scroll, and pronounces punishment on Jehoiakim and on Jerusalem and Judah for not listening.

l: scroll, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 36
s: The scroll records all the LORD's words against Israel, Judah, and the nations, written by Baruch from Jeremiah's mouth. It is read publicly, read to the princes, stored in Elishama's room, then read to the king and burned. A second scroll replaces it, with the same words plus many similar ones.

l: princes, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 36
s: The princes, including Elishama, Delaiah, Elnathan, Gemariah, and Zedekiah, hear Micaiah's report and have Baruch read the scroll to them. They turn in fear, question Baruch, tell him and Jeremiah to hide, and store the scroll in Elishama's room before telling the king. Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah plead with the king not to burn it.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 36
s: Judah's people are the intended hearers of the scroll, in hope that each will turn from his evil way and be forgiven. In the ninth month of the fifth year, people from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah gather for a fast, where Baruch reads the words. The LORD says he will bring on Judah's men the evil pronounced because they did not listen.

l: the LORD's house, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 36
s: The LORD's house is where Baruch reads the scroll to the people on the fast day, since Jeremiah is restricted from entering. The reading takes place in Gemariah's room in the upper court at the entry of the new gate.

l: burning of the scroll, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 36
s: While Jehudi reads to the king in the winter house, Jehoiakim cuts off three or four columns at a time with a penknife and throws them into the brazier until the whole scroll is consumed. He and his servants show no fear and do not tear their garments. The act leads to the LORD's command for a new scroll and his judgment on Jehoiakim.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 37
s: Zedekiah, son of Josiah, reigns in place of Coniah, but neither he nor his people heed the LORD's words through Jeremiah. Zedekiah sends Jehucal and Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to pray for them, while Pharaoh's army's approach causes the Chaldeans to withdraw from Jerusalem. The LORD tells Jeremiah that Pharaoh's army will return to Egypt and the Chaldeans will come back, take the city, and burn it. When Jeremiah goes toward Benjamin, the guard captain Irijah seizes him as a defector, and the princes beat him and imprison him in the house of Jonathan the scribe. Zedekiah secretly consults him, hears that he will be delivered to Babylon's king, and moves Jeremiah to the court of the guard, where he is given daily bread until the city's bread runs out.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 37
s: Jeremiah the prophet relays the LORD's word that Pharaoh's army will go home and the Chaldeans will return and burn Jerusalem. He is seized at Benjamin's gate by Irijah on a charge of defecting, which he denies, and is beaten and imprisoned for many days. He tells Zedekiah he will be delivered to the king of Babylon, asks not to be returned to Jonathan's house, and is placed in the court of the guard.

l: Zedekiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 37
s: Zedekiah, son of Josiah, becomes king in place of Coniah, and neither he nor his servants nor the people heed the LORD's words through Jeremiah. He sends men to ask Jeremiah to pray, later secretly asks him for a word from the LORD, and is told he will be delivered to the king of Babylon. He grants Jeremiah's plea by moving him to the court of the guard with a daily loaf of bread.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 37
s: The LORD speaks to Jeremiah, declaring that Pharaoh's army will return to Egypt and that the Chaldeans will come back, take Jerusalem, and burn it. He warns the people not to deceive themselves that the Chaldeans will depart, saying that even wounded survivors would rise up and burn the city.

l: Chaldeans, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 37
s: The Chaldeans, who were besieging Jerusalem, withdraw when they hear news of Pharaoh's army. The LORD says they will return, fight against the city, take it, and burn it with fire. Irijah accuses Jeremiah of defecting to them.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 37
s: Jerusalem is relieved when the Chaldeans withdraw from it for fear of Pharaoh's army. The LORD declares that the Chaldeans will return to take and burn it. By the end of the chapter its bread supply is running out.

l: Irijah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 37
s: Irijah, son of Shelemiah, son of Hananiah, is a captain of the guard at Benjamin's gate. He seizes Jeremiah, accusing him of defecting to the Chaldeans, ignores Jeremiah's denial, and brings him to the princes.

l: princes (Judah's princes), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 37
s: The princes are angry with Jeremiah when Irijah brings him before them. They strike him and put him in prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe, which they had made into a prison.

l: house of Jonathan the scribe, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 37
s: The house of Jonathan the scribe has been made into a prison by the princes. Jeremiah is held there in the dungeon house and cells for many days, and later pleads with Zedekiah not to be sent back lest he die there.

l: court of the guard, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 37
s: The court of the guard is where Zedekiah commands Jeremiah to be committed after the appeal. Jeremiah receives a daily loaf of bread from the bakers' street and remains there until all the city's bread is gone.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 37
s: The Chaldeans' siege of Jerusalem is lifted for a time when they withdraw on hearing of Pharaoh's army coming out of Egypt. The LORD says through Jeremiah that this is temporary, as the Chaldeans will return and take and burn the city. The closing mention of the city's bread running out points to the siege's pressure.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 38
s: Jeremiah tells the people that those who stay in Jerusalem will die while those who go out to the Chaldeans will live, and that the city will be given to the king of Babylon. Offended princes, including Shephatiah, Gedaliah, Jucal, and Pashhur, ask King Zedekiah to put him to death, and Zedekiah yields them control of him; they lower Jeremiah into Malchijah's muddy dungeon. Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a eunuch, appeals to the king, and Zedekiah orders him to take thirty men and lift Jeremiah out, which he does using cords and rags. Zedekiah then secretly questions Jeremiah, who urges him to surrender to the Babylonian princes to save his life, house, and city, but Zedekiah fears the Jews who defected. Zedekiah instructs Jeremiah to conceal their talk from the princes, and Jeremiah remains in the court of the guard until Jerusalem is taken.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 38
s: Jeremiah proclaims that staying in Jerusalem means death while going out to the Chaldeans means life, and is thrown by the princes into a dungeon where he sinks in the mire. Ebedmelech rescues him, and he then tells Zedekiah privately that surrender will save the king, his house, and the city, while refusal will bring burning and capture. He misleads the princes at the king's instruction and stays in the court of the guard until Jerusalem is taken.

l: Zedekiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 38
s: Zedekiah tells the princes that Jeremiah is in their hand and that the king cannot oppose them, but later orders Ebedmelech to rescue Jeremiah. He secretly swears not to kill Jeremiah, hears the counsel to surrender, and refuses out of fear of the defected Jews. He then tells Jeremiah to conceal their conversation from the princes.

l: Ebedmelech, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 38
s: Ebedmelech, an Ethiopian eunuch in the king's house, goes to the king at Benjamin's gate and says Jeremiah will die of famine in the dungeon. Commanded to take thirty men, he lets down rags and worn-out garments by cords for Jeremiah's armpits and lifts him out.

l: princes, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 38
s: The princes, named as Shephatiah, Gedaliah, Jucal, and Pashhur, hear Jeremiah's words and ask the king to put him to death for weakening the men of war and the people. They throw him into the dungeon, and later question him about his talk with the king, but stop speaking with him when his answer matches the king's instruction and the matter is not perceived.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 38
s: The LORD is presented as the source of Jeremiah's words that Jerusalem will be given to the king of Babylon and that those who go out to the Chaldeans will live. Zedekiah swears by the LORD, who made our souls, and Jeremiah urges him to obey the LORD's voice. Jeremiah says the LORD has shown him the fate awaiting the king's household if he refuses.

l: Chaldeans, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 38
s: The Chaldeans are the besieging army to whom Jeremiah says people should go out in order to live. Jeremiah says the city will be given into their hand and burned if Zedekiah does not surrender, and that the king's wives and children will be brought out to them.

l: king of Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 38
s: The king of Babylon is said in Jeremiah's prophecy to be the one whose army will take Jerusalem. Jeremiah warns that Zedekiah will be taken by his hand if he refuses to go out to the Babylonian princes, and that the women of the king's house will be brought out to those princes.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 38
s: Jerusalem is under siege and suffering famine, with no more bread in the city. Jeremiah says it will be given to the Chaldeans and burned unless Zedekiah surrenders, and the chapter ends noting that Jeremiah stayed in the court of the guard until the day it was taken.

l: dungeon (Malchijah's dungeon), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 38
s: The dungeon of Malchijah the king's son, located in the court of the guard, has no water but mire. Jeremiah is let down into it with cords and sinks in the mire, and is later lifted out by Ebedmelech and the thirty men.

l: Jeremiah's prophecy of Jerusalem's fall, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 38
s: Jeremiah declares that the city will surely be given into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon, who will take it. Those who remain will die by sword, famine, and pestilence, while those who go out to the Chaldeans will live. He repeats it privately to Zedekiah, offering survival and no burning if the king surrenders, and the chapter closes with Jerusalem's capture still pending.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 39
s: In the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his whole army besieged Jerusalem, and in the eleventh year a breach was made in the city and the Babylonian princes took seats in the middle gate. Zedekiah and his men of war fled by night toward the Arabah, but the Chaldean army overtook him in the plains of Jericho and brought him to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, where his sons and the nobles of Judah were killed and he was blinded and bound in fetters for transport to Babylon. The Chaldeans burned the king's house and the people's houses and broke down Jerusalem's walls, while Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried the remaining people captive to Babylon and left some of the poor in Judah with vineyards and fields. Nebuchadnezzar ordered that Jeremiah be cared for and not harmed, so Nebuzaradan and other officers took him from the court of the guard and committed him to Gedaliah, and he lived among the people. The chapter closes with a word the LORD had given Jeremiah earlier, promising Ebedmelech the Ethiopian that he would be delivered and not fall by the sword because he trusted in the LORD.

l: Zedekiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 39
s: Zedekiah king of Judah fled Jerusalem by night with his men of war through the gate between the two walls toward the Arabah, but was overtaken in the plains of Jericho and brought to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah. There his sons were killed before his eyes, his eyes were put out, and he was bound in fetters to be taken to Babylon.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 39
s: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came with all his army against Jerusalem and besieged it, then pronounced judgment on Zedekiah at Riblah, killing Zedekiah's sons and all the nobles of Judah. He also commanded Nebuzaradan to take care of Jeremiah, do him no harm, and do for him whatever he asked.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 39
s: Jerusalem was besieged from the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year, and a breach was made in the city on the ninth day of the fourth month of his eleventh year. The Chaldeans burned the king's house and the people's houses and broke down its walls.

l: Chaldeans, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 39
s: The Chaldean army pursued the fleeing Zedekiah and overtook him in the plains of Jericho, then brought him to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah. The Chaldeans also burned the king's house and the people's houses and broke down the walls of Jerusalem.

l: Babylon's army, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 39
s: Nebuchadnezzar's whole army came against Jerusalem and besieged it. After the breach, the Babylonian princes, including Nergal Sharezer, Samgarnebo, and Sarsechim the Rabsaris, entered and sat in the middle gate.

l: Nebuzaradan, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 39
s: Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried the rest of the people of the city, including the deserters, captive into Babylon, but left some of the poor who had nothing in Judah and gave them vineyards and fields. On Nebuchadnezzar's command, he joined other officers in taking Jeremiah out of the court of the guard and committing him to Gedaliah.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 39
s: Jeremiah was taken out of the court of the guard by Nebuzaradan and the other chief officers of the king of Babylon, on Nebuchadnezzar's orders that he not be harmed. He was committed to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, and lived among the people. He had also received a word from the LORD, while shut up in the court of the guard, to carry to Ebedmelech.

l: Ebedmelech, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 39
s: Ebedmelech the Ethiopian is the recipient of a message the LORD told Jeremiah to deliver. He is promised deliverance on the day the LORD's words come on the city, that he will not be given into the hand of those he fears or fall by the sword, because he has put his trust in the LORD.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 39
s: The LORD, called the LORD of Armies and the God of Israel, spoke to Jeremiah in the court of the guard, declaring that his words would come on the city for evil and not for good. He promised to surely save Ebedmelech the Ethiopian because Ebedmelech had trusted in him.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 39
s: The siege began in the tenth month of the ninth year of Zedekiah, when Nebuchadnezzar and all his army besieged the city. It ended with a breach on the ninth day of the fourth month of the eleventh year, followed by Zedekiah's flight and capture, the burning of the city's houses, the breaking of its walls, and the captivity of the remaining people.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, releases Jeremiah from his chains at Ramah and tells him the LORD brought disaster on Judah because of its sin. He offers Jeremiah the choice to go to Babylon or stay, and sends him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon made governor, at Mizpah. Gedaliah assures the captains of the forces and their men that serving the Chaldeans will bring them well-being, and Jews scattered in Moab, Ammon, Edom and other lands return and gather abundant wine and summer fruits. Johanan the son of Kareah and the captains warn Gedaliah that Baalis, king of Ammon, has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to kill him. Gedaliah does not believe them and forbids Johanan's offer to kill Ishmael secretly.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: Jeremiah is freed from chains at Ramah by Nebuzaradan after having been bound among the captives bound for Babylon. He is given the choice to go or stay, receives food and a present, and goes to live with Gedaliah at Mizpah among the people left in the land.

l: Nebuzaradan, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, releases Jeremiah from his chains and tells him the LORD brought this evil on the place because of sin and disobedience. He offers Jeremiah care in Babylon or freedom to go anywhere, directs him to Gedaliah, and sends him off with food and a present.

l: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: Gedaliah, made governor over the cities of Judah by the king of Babylon, settles at Mizpah and swears to the captains and their men that serving the Chaldeans will bring well-being. He disbelieves Johanan's warning that Ishmael means to kill him and forbids Johanan to act, saying he speaks falsely of Ishmael.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: The LORD is described by Nebuzaradan as having pronounced and brought the evil on Judah, doing as he spoke, because the people sinned against him and did not obey his voice. The chapter opens as the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD.

l: Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: The king of Babylon has made Gedaliah governor over the cities of Judah and committed to him men, women, children and the poorest of the land who were not carried captive. Many were carried captive to Babylon, and Nebuzaradan offers Jeremiah the chance to go there.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: Judah's land is under a Babylonian-appointed governor, with only a remnant and the poorest left. Jews scattered in other lands return to Judah and gather abundant wine and summer fruits.

l: Mizpah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: Mizpah is where Gedaliah dwells as governor and where Jeremiah goes to live with him. The captains, their men and returning Jews gather there, and it is where Johanan warns of the plot against Gedaliah.

l: captains of the forces, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: The captains of the forces and their men, who were in the fields, hear of Gedaliah's appointment and come to him at Mizpah, including Ishmael, Johanan, Jonathan, Seraiah, the sons of Ephai and Jezaniah. Gedaliah swears to them that serving the Chaldeans will go well, and Johanan with the captains later warns him of the plot.

l: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: Ishmael is among the captains who come to Gedaliah at Mizpah. Johanan alleges that Baalis, king of Ammon, has sent him to take Gedaliah's life, but Gedaliah rejects the claim as false.

l: Johanan the son of Kareah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: Johanan comes to Gedaliah at Mizpah with the captains and warns him of Ishmael's mission from Baalis. He privately offers to kill Ishmael secretly to protect the gathered Jews and the remnant, but Gedaliah forbids it.

l: Baalis, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: Baalis, king of the children of Ammon, is alleged by Johanan and the captains to have sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take Gedaliah's life. Gedaliah does not believe the report.

l: Jews, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: Jews in Moab, Ammon, Edom and other countries hear that the king of Babylon left a remnant and set Gedaliah over them. They return from all the places where they were driven to Judah and to Gedaliah at Mizpah, and gather very much wine and summer fruits.

l: remnant of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: The remnant of Judah consists of those not carried captive to Babylon, including men, women, children and the poorest, placed under Gedaliah. Johanan argues that Gedaliah's murder would scatter the gathered Jews and cause the remnant to perish.

l: plot to kill Gedaliah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 40
s: Johanan and the captains report that Baalis, king of Ammon, has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take Gedaliah's life. Johanan offers to kill Ishmael secretly, but Gedaliah does not believe the report and forbids it.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 41
s: In the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, a royal descendant, came with ten men to Mizpah, ate with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, and then killed him along with the Jews and Chaldean soldiers there. Two days later he lured eighty mourning pilgrims from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria into the city, killed them, and threw their bodies into the pit Asa had made, sparing ten who offered hidden stores of food. Ishmael took the remaining people of Mizpah, including the king's daughters, captive and set off toward the Ammonites. Johanan the son of Kareah and the captains heard of it, pursued him, and caught up at the great waters in Gibeon, where the captives rejoined Johanan while Ishmael escaped with eight men to the Ammonites. Johanan led the recovered remnant to Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt out of fear of the Chaldeans.

l: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 41
s: Ishmael, a royal descendant and chief officer of the king, came to Mizpah with ten men, ate with Gedaliah, and then killed him and the Jews and Chaldean soldiers there. He later deceived and killed eighty pilgrims, spared ten for their hidden stores, and took the remaining people of Mizpah captive toward the Ammonites. Johanan overtook him at Gibeon, the captives were taken back, and Ishmael escaped with eight men to the Ammonites.

l: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 41
s: Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land, hosted Ishmael and his ten men at a meal in Mizpah. Ishmael struck him down with the sword and killed him there.

l: Johanan the son of Kareah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 41
s: Johanan and the captains with him heard of Ishmael's evil, took their men, and pursued him, finding him by the great waters in Gibeon. He recovered the captives, who came over to him gladly, though Ishmael escaped. He then led the remnant to Geruth Chimham by Bethlehem, intending to enter Egypt.

l: Mizpah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 41
s: Mizpah was the place where Gedaliah was governor and where Ishmael killed him, the Jews with him, and the Chaldean men of war. Ishmael also killed pilgrims in the middle of the city and carried away the people remaining there as captives.

l: Chaldeans, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 41
s: Chaldean men of war found at Mizpah were killed by Ishmael along with Gedaliah's other companions. Afterward the people with Johanan feared the Chaldeans because Ishmael had killed the governor the king of Babylon had appointed, which motivated their plan to go to Egypt.

l: eighty men from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 41
s: These eighty men arrived with shaved beards, torn clothes, and self-inflicted cuts, carrying meal offerings and frankincense to bring to the LORD's house. Ishmael met them weeping, invited them to Gedaliah, then killed them in the middle of the city and cast them into the pit; ten of them were spared after offering hidden stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey.

l: people remaining at Mizpah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 41
s: The people left in Mizpah, including the king's daughters, had been committed to Gedaliah by Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard. Ishmael carried them away captive toward the Ammonites, but they turned back and went to Johanan when he caught up at Gibeon. The recovered remnant included men of war, women, children, and eunuchs.

l: Geruth Chimham, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 41
s: Geruth Chimham, by Bethlehem, was where Johanan and the recovered remnant went and lived after leaving Gibeon. It served as their stopping point on the way to enter Egypt.

l: Egypt, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 41
s: Egypt was the intended destination of Johanan and the remnant as they stopped at Geruth Chimham. They planned to go there because they were afraid of the Chaldeans after Gedaliah's killing.

l: Gedaliah's assassination, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 41
s: In the seventh month, Ishmael and ten men killed Gedaliah with the sword at Mizpah after eating bread with him, and also killed the Jews and Chaldean soldiers present. No one knew of it for two days, and it led to further killings, the capture of Mizpah's people, and the remnant's fear of Chaldean reprisal.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 42
s: Johanan the son of Kareah, the captains of the forces, and all the people come to Jeremiah the prophet and ask him to pray to the LORD for guidance, promising to obey whatever answer comes. After ten days the LORD's word comes to Jeremiah, who tells them that if they stay in this land the LORD will build and plant them and protect them from the king of Babylon. If they instead go to Egypt seeking to escape war and hunger, the sword, famine, and pestilence will overtake them there and they will die. Jeremiah warns that they have dealt deceitfully with their own souls by asking for the word while not intending to obey it, and he repeats that they will die in the place where they wish to live.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 42
s: Jeremiah is asked by the people to pray to the LORD for them, and he promises to keep nothing back from his report. After ten days he receives the LORD's word and delivers it, telling the remnant to stay in the land and not go to Egypt. He charges them with dealing deceitfully against their own souls and declares that they will die by sword, famine, and pestilence in Egypt.

l: Johanan the son of Kareah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 42
s: Johanan the son of Kareah, together with the captains and all the people, approaches Jeremiah to request a prayer for guidance. He is among those Jeremiah calls together to hear the LORD's answer.

l: captains of the forces, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 42
s: The captains of the forces join Johanan and the people in asking Jeremiah to pray to the LORD for the way they should walk. They are summoned with Johanan to hear the LORD's response.

l: remnant of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 42
s: The remnant, left a few out of many, asks for the LORD's direction and swears to obey whether the answer is good or bad. The LORD then tells them to stay in the land, promising to build and plant them, but warns that going to Egypt will bring death and that they will see this place no more. Jeremiah says they have been deceitful and have not obeyed in anything he was sent to tell them.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 42
s: The LORD answers through Jeremiah after ten days, promising to build and plant the remnant if they stay and saying he grieves over the distress he has brought on them. He promises to be with them to save them from the king of Babylon and to grant them mercy. If they go to Egypt, he says his wrath will be poured out on them as it was on Jerusalem and they will become an object of horror, a curse, and a reproach.

l: king of Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 42
s: The king of Babylon is the one the people fear. The LORD tells them twice not to be afraid of him, promising to save them from his hand and to grant mercy so that he will have mercy on them and let them return to their own land.

l: Egypt, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 42
s: Egypt is the place the people intend to go, believing they will see no war, hear no trumpet, and lack no bread there. The LORD declares that going there will bring the sword, famine, and death instead, and Jeremiah says 'Don't go into Egypt!'

l: this land (Judah), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 42
s: The land is where the LORD says the remnant should keep living, promising to build and plant them there and not pull down or pluck up. The people's saying 'We will not dwell in this land' is described as disobedience to the LORD's voice. Going to Egypt means they will see this place no more.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 43
s: After Jeremiah finishes delivering the LORD's words, Azariah, Johanan the son of Kareah, and the proud men accuse him of speaking falsely and claim Baruch the son of Neriah has turned him against them to hand them over to the Chaldeans. Johanan and the captains disobey the LORD's voice and take the whole remnant of Judah, including Jeremiah and Baruch, into Egypt, where they arrive at Tahpanhes. There the LORD tells Jeremiah to hide great stones in the brickwork at the entry of Pharaoh's house in sight of the men of Judah. He explains that he will bring Nebuchadnezzar, his servant, to set his throne on those stones. Nebuchadnezzar will strike Egypt with death, captivity, and the sword, burn the houses of Egypt's gods, and break the pillars of Beth Shemesh.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 43
s: Jeremiah finishes speaking all the LORD's words to the people and is accused by Azariah, Johanan, and the proud men of speaking falsely. He is taken into Egypt with the remnant and arrives at Tahpanhes. There the LORD's word comes to him, commanding him to hide great stones in the brickwork at the entry of Pharaoh's house and to announce Nebuchadnezzar's coming.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 43
s: The LORD is said by Jeremiah to have sent him with words forbidding the move to Egypt, and the people refuse to obey his voice. At Tahpanhes he instructs Jeremiah to hide stones and declares he will send for Nebuchadnezzar, his servant, to set his throne on them. He promises to kindle a fire in the houses of Egypt's gods.

l: Johanan the son of Kareah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 43
s: Johanan joins Azariah and the proud men in calling Jeremiah a liar. He and the captains of the forces then disobey the LORD's voice and lead the remnant of Judah, with Jeremiah and Baruch, into Egypt as far as Tahpanhes.

l: Baruch the son of Neriah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 43
s: Baruch is accused by Azariah, Johanan, and the proud men of turning Jeremiah against them in order to deliver them to the Chaldeans to be killed or carried captive to Babylon. He is among those taken into Egypt and arrives at Tahpanhes.

l: Egypt, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 43
s: Egypt is where the remnant of Judah goes in disobedience to the LORD. The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar will strike it, so that some are put to death, some taken captive, and some killed by the sword. He will burn the houses of its gods, carry the gods away, and break the pillars of Beth Shemesh there.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 43
s: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is called the LORD's servant, whom the LORD will send for and take. His throne will be set on the hidden stones, and he will spread his royal pavilion over them. He will strike Egypt, burn its gods' houses, array himself with the land as a shepherd puts on a garment, and leave in peace.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 43
s: The land of Judah is where the LORD's voice told the people to dwell, but Johanan, the captains, and the people refuse to obey and do not stay. The remnant had returned to it from all the nations where they had been driven, and it is now left for Egypt.

l: remnant of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 43
s: The remnant of Judah had returned from all the nations where they had been driven to live in Judah. Johanan and the captains take them, the men, women, children, and king's daughters, into Egypt in disobedience to the LORD. The people include those Nebuzaradan had left with Gedaliah, and they reach Tahpanhes.

l: Tahpanhes, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 43
s: Tahpanhes in Egypt is where the remnant of Judah arrives after disobeying the LORD's voice. It is where the LORD's word comes to Jeremiah, and it contains Pharaoh's house, at whose entry the stones are to be hidden.

l: great stones, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 43
s: Jeremiah is commanded to take great stones and hide them in mortar in the brickwork at the entry of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes, in sight of the men of Judah. The LORD says he will set Nebuchadnezzar's throne on these stones, and the king will spread his royal pavilion over them.

l: Babylon's conquest of Egypt, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 43
s: The LORD declares that Nebuchadnezzar will come and strike Egypt, with some put to death, some taken into captivity, and some killed by the sword. He will burn and carry away the gods of Egypt and break the pillars of Beth Shemesh. This is foretold through Jeremiah's act with the stones at Tahpanhes.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 44
s: Jeremiah delivers the word of the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, to all the Jews living in Egypt at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, and Pathros. He recalls that Jerusalem and the cities of Judah are desolate because of idolatrous incense burning, despite repeated warnings from the prophets, and warns that the Judah remnant in Egypt will be consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence. The men and women refuse to listen, vowing to keep burning incense and pouring drink offerings to the queen of the sky, claiming prosperity came with it and hardship came when they stopped. Jeremiah answers that the LORD remembered their incense and brought the desolation, and he tells them to go ahead and keep their vows, while the LORD swears that his name will no longer be invoked by the men of Judah in Egypt. The LORD gives a sign: he will give Pharaoh Hophra into the hand of his enemies, as he gave Zedekiah to Nebuchadnezzar, and only a few escapees will return to Judah.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 44
s: Jeremiah receives and delivers the LORD's word to all the Jews in Egypt, rebuking their idolatry and warning of destruction. When the people and women reject him, he replies that the LORD brought the desolation of Judah because of their incense burning, and he proclaims the LORD's oath and the sign concerning Pharaoh Hophra.

l: Jews living in Egypt (Judah remnant), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 44
s: The Jews living in Egypt, at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, and Pathros, are accused of repeating the sins of their fathers and kings. They refuse to listen to Jeremiah and insist on continuing to worship the queen of the sky, and the LORD says they will be consumed by sword and famine, with only a few escapees returning to Judah.

l: women (of the Jews in Egypt), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 44
s: The women stand in the great assembly that answers Jeremiah, and they argue that they made cakes and poured drink offerings to the queen of the sky with their husbands' knowledge. Jeremiah addresses them directly with the men, saying their vows are fulfilled by mouth and hand, and the LORD's word applies to them as well.

l: queen of the sky, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 44
s: The queen of the sky is the deity to whom the Jews in Egypt, like their fathers, kings, and princes, burn incense and pour drink offerings, and for whom the women make cakes. The people claim they prospered while worshiping her and lacked all things once they stopped.

l: Egypt, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 44
s: Egypt is where the Judah remnant went to live and where they continue burning incense to other gods. The LORD says he will punish those dwelling there as he punished Jerusalem, and that Pharaoh Hophra, its king, will be given into the hand of his enemies.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 44
s: Jerusalem is cited as a place of evil the LORD brought down, now a desolation where no man dwells, because of the idolatrous incense burning in its streets. Its fate is the model for what will come on those in Egypt.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 44
s: Judah's cities are described as wasted and desolate because of the people's wickedness and incense to other gods. The remnant that fled to Egypt is threatened with being cut off, and only a few who escape will return to the land of Judah.

l: idolatrous incense burning and drink offerings, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 44
s: Burning incense and pouring drink offerings to other gods, specifically the queen of the sky, is the abomination that provoked the LORD's anger in Judah and Jerusalem and continues in Egypt. The people vow to continue it, and Jeremiah says the LORD remembered it and could no longer bear it.

l: sword, famine, and pestilence, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 44
s: Sword, famine, and pestilence are the means by which the LORD says he punished Jerusalem and will punish those in Egypt. The Judah remnant there will be consumed by sword and famine from the least to the greatest, becoming an object of horror, a curse, and a reproach.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 45
s: Chapter 45 records a message that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, when Baruch was writing Jeremiah's words in a book. The LORD, the God of Israel, quotes Baruch's complaint that He has added sorrow to his pain and that he is weary with groaning and finds no rest.
