The LORD declares that He will break down what He has built and pluck up what He has planted throughout the whole land. He asks whether Baruch seeks great things for himself and tells him not to, since evil will come on all flesh. The LORD promises that Baruch will escape with his life wherever he goes.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 45
s: Jeremiah the prophet speaks the LORD's message to Baruch in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, king of Judah. Baruch writes Jeremiah's words in a book at his mouth.

l: Baruch the son of Neriah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 45
s: Baruch writes Jeremiah's words in a book and is the recipient of the LORD's message in the fourth year of Jehoiakim. He is told not to seek great things for himself, and is promised that he will escape with his life wherever he goes.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 45
s: The LORD, the God of Israel, answers Baruch's lament through Jeremiah. He declares that He will break down what He has built and pluck up what He has planted in the whole land, and that He will bring evil on all flesh. He promises Baruch his life as a reward, wherever he goes.

l: coming judgment (the LORD's breaking down and plucking up), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 45
s: The LORD announces that what He has built He will break down and what He has planted He will pluck up, throughout the whole land. He says He will bring evil on all flesh, with Baruch alone singled out to escape with his life.

l: Baruch's lament (sorrow and weariness), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 45
s: Baruch had cried, "Woe is me now!", saying the LORD had added sorrow to his pain and that he was weary with groaning and found no rest. The LORD answers it by telling him not to seek great things for himself and by promising him his life.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 46
s: Chapter 46 is the LORD's word to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations, beginning with Egypt. It describes the defeat of Pharaoh Necoh's army at Carchemish by the Euphrates, struck by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon in the fourth year of Jehoiakim of Judah. Egypt's boast of rising like the Nile is answered with a day of vengeance for the LORD, no healing for Egypt, and a coming invasion by Nebuchadnezzar's innumerable army from the north that will devastate Memphis and other cities and hand Egypt, Amon of No, and Pharaoh over to captivity. The LORD adds that Egypt will afterwards be inhabited as in the days of old. He then comforts Jacob his servant, promising to save him from captivity, to be with him, and to correct him in measure without leaving him unpunished.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 46
s: The LORD gives Jeremiah a word concerning the nations, declaring that the day of Egypt's defeat is his day of vengeance and that he pushed Egypt's strong ones so they fell. He promises to punish Amon of No, Pharaoh, Egypt, her gods and kings, and to deliver them to Nebuchadnezzar, though Egypt will later be inhabited again. He assures Jacob he will save him from captivity, make a full end of the nations where he drove him but not of Jacob, and correct him in measure.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 46
s: Jeremiah the prophet receives the LORD's word concerning the nations, specifically Egypt. He is also told how Nebuchadnezzar will come and strike the land of Egypt.

l: Egypt, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 46
s: Egypt boasts of rising like the Nile to cover the earth and destroy cities, but is defeated, with no healing for her, and is portrayed as a beautiful heifer facing destruction out of the north. Memphis will become a desolation, and Egypt will be delivered into the hand of the people of the north and of Nebuchadnezzar, though afterwards it will be inhabited as in the days of old.

l: Pharaoh Necoh, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 46
s: Pharaoh Necoh is named as king of Egypt whose army was by the Euphrates in Carchemish. Egyptians later say Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise who has let the appointed time pass by, and the LORD declares he will punish Pharaoh and those who trust in him.

l: army of Pharaoh Necoh, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 46
s: The army of Pharaoh Necoh is called to prepare shield, horses, and spears for battle, but is dismayed, turns backward, and its mighty ones are beaten down and flee without looking back. They stumble and fall in the north by the Euphrates, and the mighty fall against one another.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 46
s: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck Pharaoh Necoh's army at Carchemish in the fourth year of Jehoiakim. The LORD says he will come and strike the land of Egypt, and the LORD will deliver Egypt's people into his hand and the hands of his servants.

l: Babylon's army, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 46
s: The invaders from the north are described as marching with axes like woodcutters and cutting down Egypt's forest, being more numerous than locusts and innumerable. Their sound is likened to a serpent, and they are the people of the north into whose hand Egypt is delivered.

l: Jacob, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 46
s: Jacob, also called Israel, the LORD's servant, is told not to be afraid or dismayed. The LORD will save him and his offspring from the land of captivity, and Jacob will return and be quiet and at ease, though the LORD will correct him in measure and not leave him unpunished.

l: Egypt's defeat at Carchemish, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 46
s: Egypt's army was struck by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish by the river Euphrates in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah. The defeat is depicted as a rout in which the mighty stumbled and fell, and as a sacrifice the Lord GOD of Armies holds in the north country on a day of vengeance.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 47
s: Chapter 47 records the LORD's word to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, given before Pharaoh struck Gaza. The LORD describes waters rising out of the north that become an overflowing stream flooding the land, its cities and inhabitants, so that men cry out and all wail. The noise of the hoofs, chariots, and wheels of the invader's strong ones makes fathers too feeble to look back for their children. The day is coming to destroy all the Philistines and cut off every remaining helper from Tyre and Sidon, and Gaza and Ashkelon are described as bald and brought to nothing. The chapter ends with an address to the sword of the LORD, which asks how long until it is quiet, and is answered that it cannot rest because the LORD has commanded it against Ashkelon and the seashore.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 47
s: The LORD gives Jeremiah the prophet a word concerning the Philistines and announces the flood from the north and the day of destruction. He declares that he will destroy the Philistines, the remnant of the isle of Caphtor, and that he has given the sword a command and appointed it against Ashkelon and the seashore.

l: Philistines, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 47
s: The Philistines are the subject of the LORD's word to Jeremiah, which was given before Pharaoh struck Gaza. A day is coming to destroy all of them and to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every remaining helper, and they are called the remnant of the isle of Caphtor.

l: Gaza, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 47
s: Gaza is named as the place Pharaoh struck, which dates the word to Jeremiah. Baldness is said to have come on Gaza.

l: Ashkelon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 47
s: Ashkelon is said to be brought to nothing. It is also the target against which the LORD has appointed his sword, along with the seashore.

l: overflowing waters from the north, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 47
s: Waters rise up out of the north and become an overflowing stream. They overflow the land and all that is in it, the city and those who dwell there, so that men cry out and all the inhabitants wail.

l: advancing army (the northern invader), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 47
s: The invader is described through the stamping of the hoofs of his strong ones, the rushing of his chariots, and the rumbling of his wheels. The noise leaves fathers unable to look back for their children because their hands are so feeble.

l: sword of the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 47
s: The sword of the LORD is asked how long it will be before it is quiet and is told to return to its scabbard, rest, and be still. The reply is that it cannot be quiet because the LORD has commanded it and appointed it against Ashkelon and the seashore.

l: destruction of the Philistines, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 47
s: A coming day is announced to destroy all the Philistines and to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper who remains. The LORD himself will carry it out, and signs of it include Gaza's baldness, Ashkelon being brought to nothing, and the remnant of their valley cutting themselves in mourning.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 48
s: Chapter 48 is the LORD of Armies' oracle against Moab, announcing the destruction of its cities, including Nebo, Kiriathaim, Heshbon, Dibon, and Kerioth. Moab is judged for trusting in its works and treasures, for its long complacency, and for its pride and for magnifying itself against the LORD. Its god Chemosh will go into captivity with his priests and princes, and a destroyer will come on every city so that none escapes. The LORD himself laments for Moab's vineyards and people, even as he promises terror, the pit, and the snare, and an end to its being a people. The chapter closes with a promise that the LORD will reverse Moab's captivity in the latter days.

l: Moab, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 48
s: Moab is laid waste: its cities are taken, its young men slaughtered, its fields and vineyards stripped of joy, and its people mourn and flee. It had been at ease from its youth and trusted in its works and treasures, and it is to be destroyed as a people for magnifying itself against the LORD. Its captivity will nevertheless be reversed in the latter days.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 48
s: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel and the King, speaks the oracle against Moab, curses those who do the work negligently or hold back the sword, and sends the destroyer. He also says he will wail and weep for Moab, and he promises to reverse its captivity in the latter days.

l: Chemosh, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 48
s: Chemosh, the god of Moab, will go out into captivity with his priests and princes together. Moab will be ashamed of him as Israel was ashamed of Bethel, and his people are called undone.

l: destroyer (of Moab), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 48
s: The destroyer will come on every city of Moab so that none escapes, and the valley and plain will perish. He has come up against Dibon and destroyed its strongholds, and he has fallen on Moab's summer fruits and vintage.

l: judgment of Moab, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 48
s: The judgment has come on the plain country and all the cities of Moab, far or near, and Moab's horn is cut off and its arm broken. It includes terror, the pit, and the snare, with the year of visitation, and the chapter ends by saying that thus far is the judgment of Moab.

l: pride of Moab, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 48
s: Moab's pride, loftiness, and arrogance are said to have been heard of, and the LORD declares that its wrath and boastings are nothing and have done nothing. This pride, in magnifying itself against the LORD, is given as a reason Moab will be made drunk, become a derision, and be destroyed as a people.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 49
s: Jeremiah 49 records the LORD's oracles of judgment against several nations. Ammon, whose god Malcam occupies Gad, will see Rabbah become a desolate heap, yet its captivity is later reversed. Edom, including Teman, Dedan and Bozrah, is stripped bare, made small, and brought down from its heights like Sodom and Gomorrah. Damascus, Kedar, and Hazor are threatened with terror, flight and desolation, with Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon named as the agent against Kedar and Hazor. Elam is to have its bow broken and be scattered to all the winds, but its captivity will be reversed in the latter days.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 49
s: The LORD pronounces judgment on Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Hazor, and Elam, swearing by himself against Bozrah and declaring that no one can appoint him a time. He promises to preserve Edom's fatherless children and widows, and to reverse the captivity of Ammon and Elam in later days.

l: Ammon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 49
s: Ammon is rebuked because Malcam possesses Gad and its people dwell in Gad's cities. The LORD says Rabbah will become a desolate heap, its daughters burned, Malcam will go into captivity with his priests and princes, and Ammon will be driven out for trusting in its treasures. Afterward the LORD will reverse Ammon's captivity.

l: Edom, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 49
s: Edom, including Teman, Dedan and Bozrah, is judged: its wisdom fails, Esau is made bare and his hidden places uncovered, and his offspring and neighbors are destroyed. The LORD will bring it down from its rocky heights despite its pride, make it an astonishment like Sodom and Gomorrah with no one dwelling there, and make its mighty men like a woman in labor. Its fatherless children and widows are to be preserved by the LORD.

l: Damascus, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 49
s: Damascus grows feeble, flees, and is seized by trembling and anguish like a woman in travail, while Hamath and Arpad are confounded by bad news. Its young men will fall in its streets and its men of war be silenced. The LORD will kindle a fire in its wall that devours the palaces of Ben Hadad.

l: Kedar, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 49
s: Kedar is described as struck by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and the LORD commands an attack on the children of the east. Their tents, flocks, curtains, vessels and camels are to be carried off as they are met with cries of 'Terror on every side!' The LORD will scatter them to all winds and bring calamity from every side.

l: Hazor, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 49
s: The kingdoms of Hazor are struck by Nebuchadnezzar, and its inhabitants are told to flee and dwell in the depths because he has planned against them. Hazor is described as a nation at ease without gates or bars, whose camels and livestock become plunder. It will become a dwelling place of jackals, a perpetual desolation where no one lives.

l: Elam, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 49
s: In the word given to Jeremiah at the start of Zedekiah's reign, the LORD says he will break Elam's bow, scatter its people to the four winds, and send the sword after them until they are consumed. He will set his throne in Elam and destroy its king and princes. In the latter days he will reverse Elam's captivity.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 49
s: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is named as the one who struck Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor. He is said to have taken counsel and conceived a purpose against the inhabitants of Hazor.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 50
s: Chapter 50 records the word the LORD spoke through Jeremiah the prophet against Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans. A nation from the north, with a company of great nations and many kings, is stirred up to take Babylon, make it desolate, and destroy its idols, its warriors, its wise men and its waters, because it has been proud against the LORD and plundered his heritage. Israel and Judah, described as lost sheep misled by their shepherds and devoured by Assyria and Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, are told to flee Babylon, return weeping to seek the LORD in an everlasting covenant, and be pardoned as a remnant. The LORD, their strong Redeemer, will plead their cause and bring Israel back to Carmel, Bashan, Ephraim and Gilead. The chapter ends with Babylon's king losing heart and the earth trembling at the noise of Babylon's capture.

l: Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 50
s: Babylon is declared taken, with Bel and Merodach dismayed and its images disappointed. It is condemned for pride, for plundering the LORD's heritage, and for devotion to idols, and is to be repaid as it has done, left desolate and uninhabited forever like Sodom and Gomorrah. Its king grows feeble at the news of the coming enemy, and the earth trembles at its capture.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 50
s: The LORD speaks through Jeremiah, stirring up the northern nations, opening his armory, and laying a snare for Babylon because it fought against him. He is the strong Redeemer of Israel and Judah who pleads their cause, pardons the remnant he leaves, and brings Israel back to its pasture. No shepherd can stand before him or appoint him a time.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 50
s: Israel is portrayed as a hunted and lost sheep, devoured first by the king of Assyria and then with bones broken by Nebuchadnezzar. The LORD promises to bring Israel back to Carmel, Bashan, the hills of Ephraim and Gilead, and to pardon its iniquity so that none is found. Israel will come weeping with Judah to seek the LORD in an everlasting covenant.

l: Judah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 50
s: Judah's children come together with the children of Israel, weeping, to seek the LORD and inquire toward Zion. Judah's sins will be sought and not found, for the LORD will pardon the remnant he leaves. Judah is also described as oppressed with Israel by captors who refuse to release them.

l: Chaldeans, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 50
s: The Chaldeans' land is to become a prey, and the LORD has a work to do there. A sword is to fall on the Chaldeans, the inhabitants of Babylon, her princes, wise men, boasters, mighty men, horses, chariots and treasures. They are told that Chaldea will be plundered and that the LORD will punish its king and land.

l: nation from the north (against Babylon), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 50
s: A nation comes up out of the north against Babylon, along with a company of great nations and many kings from the uttermost parts of the earth. They are expert archers, cruel and merciless, riding horses in array with a voice roaring like the sea. They make Babylon's land desolate, and the LORD stirs them up to carry out his purposes.

l: Babylon's destruction, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 50
s: The fall of Babylon is announced as already taken: its bulwarks fall, its walls are thrown down, and it becomes a desolation among the nations. It is the LORD's vengeance for Babylon's pride and treatment of his people, and its land is left uninhabited like Sodom and Gomorrah. The noise of its capture makes the earth tremble, and the cry is heard among the nations.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 51
s: In Jeremiah 51 the LORD declares that he will destroy Babylon, the cup that made the nations drunk, by sending destroyers and stirring up the kings of the Medes. Israel and Judah are told they are not forsaken, and his people are urged to flee Babylon and declare the LORD's work in Zion. The chapter contrasts the LORD, creator of the earth, with the worthless idols of goldsmiths, and calls Babylon his battle ax before turning the weapon against her. Zion and Jerusalem cry out against Nebuchadnezzar's violence, and the LORD promises vengeance, drying up her sea and judging Bel. Jeremiah then commands Seraiah to read his book of Babylon's doom there, bind a stone to it, and cast it into the Euphrates as a sign that Babylon will sink and not rise.

l: Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 51
s: Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand that made all the earth drunk, but is now declared fallen, unhealed, and doomed to desolation. Its walls, gates, mighty men, princes, and idols are to be overthrown, and its land left without inhabitant like heaps and a dwelling for jackals. Its king Nebuchadnezzar is accused of devouring Zion.

l: the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 51
s: The LORD, called the LORD of Armies and the God of Israel, vows vengeance on Babylon, swearing by himself and pleading the cause of Zion. He is presented as creator of the earth, heavens, and weather, in contrast to lifeless idols. He is also called a God of retribution who will surely repay.

l: Chaldeans, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 51
s: The Chaldeans are the people of Babylon, whose slain will fall in their land and streets. They are to be repaid for all the evil they did in Zion, and their inhabitants are to be made drunk and sleep a perpetual sleep.

l: Israel, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 51
s: Israel and Judah are said not to be forsaken by their God, though their land is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel. Babylon has made Israel's slain fall, so Babylon's slain will fall in return. Zion and Jerusalem cry out for vengeance, and Israel's people are told to flee Babylon and remember the LORD and Jerusalem.

l: Medes, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 51
s: The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, along with their governors and deputies, to be prepared against Babylon. Their rising fulfills his purpose to destroy it as vengeance for his temple.

l: Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 51
s: Jeremiah the prophet wrote in a book all the evil that would come on Babylon. He commanded Seraiah to read it in Babylon and then sink it in the Euphrates. The chapter closes with the note that these are the words of Jeremiah.

l: Seraiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 51
s: Seraiah, son of Neriah and chief quartermaster, went with King Zedekiah to Babylon in Zedekiah's fourth year. Jeremiah charged him to read the book aloud there, pray that the LORD will make the place desolate forever, bind a stone to the book, and cast it into the Euphrates.

l: book (Jeremiah's book against Babylon), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 51
s: Jeremiah wrote in this book all the evil that would come on Babylon. Seraiah is to read it in Babylon, then bind a stone to it and throw it into the middle of the Euphrates. Its sinking symbolizes Babylon sinking and not rising again.

l: destroyers (against Babylon), The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 51
s: Destroyers are sent by the LORD against Babylon, described as a destroying wind, strangers who winnow her, and men like locusts. They come from the north, and even if Babylon mounts to the sky they will reach her. They take her mighty men and break their bows.

l: Babylon's destruction, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 51
s: Babylon's destruction is portrayed as the LORD's purposed vengeance: sudden fall, fire on her dwellings and gates, a flood of the sea, and drying of her fountain. Her land becomes a perpetual desolation without inhabitant, and the nations will no longer flow to Bel. It is sealed by the symbolic sinking of the book in the Euphrates.

l: The Book of Jeremiah, The Book of Jeremiah, Chapter 52
s: Chapter 52 recounts the fall of Jerusalem under Zedekiah, who did evil, rebelled against the king of Babylon, and was captured after Nebuchadnezzar besieged the city from the ninth to the eleventh year of his reign. Zedekiah's sons and the princes of Judah were killed, Zedekiah was blinded and imprisoned in Babylon, and Nebuzaradan burned the LORD's house, the king's house and all the great houses, and broke down the walls. The Chaldeans broke up and carried off the temple's bronze pillars, sea, bases and vessels, and Nebuzaradan took leading priests and officials to Riblah, where the king of Babylon put them to death. The chapter lists the captives carried away in three deportations, totaling four thousand six hundred. It ends with Evilmerodach king of Babylon releasing Jehoiachin from prison in the thirty-seventh year of his captivity, treating him kindly and providing for him daily until his death.
